text: The AST 101 observing night is on Friday of week 2, from 8 to 10 pm, on the north lawn behind the science building. It counts as observing log entry 4. Come for any part of it; thirty minutes is enough for the log entry. If the sky is cloudy at 6 pm, the night moves to Monday at the same time, and the course page will say so by 6:30 pm.

Warm clothes, even if the afternoon was warm: standing still at night is cold. A pencil, your observing log, and a flashlight covered with red cellophane or a red filter. White light ruins everyone's night vision for about twenty minutes, so please keep phone screens dim and red-tinted. Binoculars are welcome but not needed.

Stay on the lawn and away from the parking lot. Walk, do not run, near the telescopes and their tripods. Never point a telescope or binoculars at the Sun, even near sunset, without a proper solar filter installed by an instructor; it can blind you instantly. Laser pointers are used only by the instructors.

Depending on the sky: the Moon, ideally near first quarter, where the shadows along the line between light and dark show craters best; any bright planet that is up; the Big Dipper and Polaris; the double star Mizar and Alcor in the Dipper's handle; the Pleiades star cluster; and, if it is dark enough, the Andromeda galaxy, a faint smudge about 2.5 million light-years away.

An instructor will aim each telescope. Look without touching the eyepiece or the tube; a small bump moves the view far off target. Use the focus knob gently if the view is blurry. Notice that stars stay points of light at any magnification, while the Moon and planets show detail. Ask why.

For entry 4, record the date, time, sky conditions and at least two targets. For each target make a quick sketch and write two or three sentences: what you expected to see, what you actually saw, and one question it raised. Measure one angle with your hand, such as the Moon's height above the horizon.
